stem: A 40-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 8 years ago presents with 6 months of progressively worsening exertional dyspnea, now NYHA III, and one episode of exertional syncope last week. Vital signs: BP 108/68 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, SpO2 92% on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals a loud P2, a left parasternal heave, and prominent jugular v-waves. Lung exam is clear; CT chest is normal (no parenchymal lung disease, no thromboembolic disease). V/Q scan is normal (no segmental perfusion defects). Echocardiogram shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle with septal flattening and an estimated pulmonary-artery systolic pressure of 60 mmHg; left ventricular function is normal and there is no significant valvular disease. Right-heart catheterization confirms PRECAPILLARY pulmonary hypertension: mean pulmonary-artery pressure 42 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 8 mmHg, and pulmonary vascular resistance 6 Wood units. There is no evidence of left heart disease, parenchymal lung disease, or chronic thromboembolic disease. The diagnosis is SLE-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension (Group 1 PAH).
question: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: PAH-specific therapy (initial monotherapy with a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor or endothelin-receptor antagonist; consider upfront combination per the AMBITION trial in selected patients) PLUS immunosuppression for SLE (corticosteroids + IV cyclophosphamide per case-series evidence) PLUS supportive care PLUS referral to a pulmonary-hypertension center
options.B: IV cyclophosphamide alone — the underlying SLE inflammation drives the PAH; PAH-specific vasodilators are not needed
options.C: Optimize heart-failure management for postcapillary pulmonary hypertension (do NOT initiate PAH-specific vasodilators because they may worsen pulmonary edema in left-heart-disease-driven PH); diuresis, GDMT for HFpEF, treat comorbidities

rationale: SLE-associated PAH is classified as WHO Group 1 PAH (associated with connective-tissue disease) per the 2022 ESC/ERS Pulmonary Hypertension Guidelines. Confirmed precapillary PH on right-heart catheterization (mean PAP ≥20 mmHg + PCWP ≤15 mmHg + PVR >2 Wood units) in the absence of left heart disease, parenchymal lung disease, or chronic thromboembolic disease establishes the Group 1 designation. Treatment requires both: (1) PAH-specific vasodilator therapy (initial monotherapy with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor — sildenafil or tadalafil — or endothelin-receptor antagonist — ambrisentan, bosentan, macitentan; the AMBITION trial supports upfront combination of ambrisentan + tadalafil in selected patients with idiopathic, heritable, drug-induced, or CTD-associated PAH); (2) immunosuppression for the underlying SLE inflammation (corticosteroids + IV cyclophosphamide induction per published case-series; some centers add MMF) — distinct from idiopathic PAH where immunosuppression is not standard; (3) supportive care (diuretics, oxygen, anticoagulation in selected patients) and (4) referral to an experienced PH center. Cyclophosphamide alone (option B) misses the vasodilator component. The HFpEF option (option C) is the management for postcapillary PH (Group 2) — but this patient has confirmed precapillary PH on RHC. PDE5 alone without immunosuppression (option D) misses the SLE inflammatory component.

variants.stem_override: A 75-year-old woman with longstanding SLE (15 years), hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity (BMI 34), and atrial fibrillation presents with progressive exertional dyspnea (NYHA III) and lower-extremity edema. Vital signs: BP 138/82, HR 84 bpm. Echocardiogram shows preserved LVEF (60%), mildly thickened LV walls, biatrial enlargement, grade II diastolic dysfunction, an elevated estimated pulmonary-artery systolic pressure of 50 mmHg, and a dilated right ventricle. Right-heart catheterization shows POSTCAPILLARY pulmonary hypertension: mean pulmonary-artery pressure 30 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 22 mmHg (elevated, consistent with left heart disease), pulmonary vascular resistance 1.8 Wood units. The diagnosis is HFpEF with secondary postcapillary pulmonary hypertension (Group 2 PH).
variants.rationale_for_variant: Mixed perturbation — entirely different etiology of pulmonary hypertension. Postcapillary (Group 2) PH from left-heart disease is treated by managing the underlying left-sided pathology (HFpEF: diuresis, BP control, SGLT2 inhibitor per EMPEROR-Preserved/DELIVER, treatment of comorbidities like AFib and obesity). PAH-specific vasodilators (PDE5 inhibitors, endothelin-receptor antagonists, prostacyclin analogs) are NOT recommended in Group 2 PH and may WORSEN outcomes by increasing left-atrial filling and pulmonary edema. The correct answer therefore shifts from PAH-specific therapy + immunosuppression (option A) to optimization of HFpEF management (option C).

variants.stem_override: A 45-year-old man with systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 6 years ago presents with 6 months of progressively worsening exertional dyspnea (NYHA III) and one episode of exertional syncope. Vital signs: BP 108/68, HR 96, SpO2 92% on room air. Cardiac exam shows a loud P2 and a left parasternal heave. Lung exam is clear; CT chest normal; V/Q scan normal. Echocardiogram shows dilated hypokinetic right ventricle with estimated PASP 60 mmHg; LV function normal. Right-heart catheterization confirms precapillary PH: mPAP 42 mmHg, PCWP 8 mmHg, PVR 6 Wood units. SLE-associated PAH (Group 1).
variants.rationale_for_variant: Sex perturbation only — clinical context (SLE-associated Group 1 PAH confirmed by RHC) is unchanged. SLE-associated PAH is approximately 9× more common in women than men (mirroring the SLE sex ratio), but the management approach (PAH-specific vasodilator + immunosuppression + supportive care + PH-center referral) is sex-independent.
